fun_facts: Phoenix's street grid was originally laid out in 1870 on a perfect north-south axis, making it one of the most regular grids in the US.
The Valley of the Sun's grid system covers over 500 square miles, making it one of the largest in the world by area.
Many of Phoenix's major roads are exactly one mile apart — a legacy of the federal land survey system used to settle the West.
Chicago's famous grid system is anchored at State & Madison Streets — the zero point from which all addresses in the city are measured.
The Chicago River was reversed in 1900 to flow away from Lake Michigan, and the lakefront roadway (Lake Shore Drive) curves along the shore in a way that breaks the city's otherwise rigid grid.
The diagonal streets cutting through Chicago — like Milwaukee Ave and Clark St — follow old Native American trading trails that predate the city's formal grid.
Boston's famously winding streets are often said to follow old cow paths, though historians note the real cause is centuries of organic urban growth from the 1630s onward.
The Big Dig, completed in 2007, buried the I-93 highway underground through the heart of the city — dramatically changing Boston's surface street layout.
Boston's street network is so complex that GPS systems regularly fail in the older neighborhoods; locals navigate largely by landmark.
Denver's downtown grid is rotated 45 degrees from the cardinal directions, aligned with the South Platte River rather than true north-south.
Colfax Avenue, running diagonally through Denver, is one of the longest commercial streets in the US at over 26 miles.
Denver's street naming follows a unique system: streets east of Broadway are numbered, while streets west use names — a relic of two separately platted 19th-century towns that merged.
Portland's blocks are famously tiny — just 200 feet square, about one-quarter the size of a typical American city block — making it one of the most walkable grids in the country.
The Willamette River divides Portland into east and west halves, each with its own grid system that doesn't quite line up at the bridges.
Portland has more bridges per capita than any other US city, with 12 bridges crossing the Willamette within the city limits.
